reference_opening.argument: This video is scam content because it actively promotes paying about $10,000 for a StrongBlock node while presenting $100 per day in passive income as a probable outcome and describing the setup as something that 'prints money.' The creator recommends buying nodes, claims he will buy more, and invites viewers to DM him to partner on a node, making the income claim a direct solicitation rather than neutral commentary. The video also directs viewers to pay $9 per month for buy-and-sell alerts tied to its crypto earning opportunities.

citations.quote: how you can make $100 a day completely passive with a strong note
if you have the money i strongly recommend looking into this because this actually prints money this is an insane money maker
if you want me to run a node for you, all you got to do is send me an Instagram DM
Literally it's $9 a month guys you can sign up down below
you would need to contribute ten of the strong tokens to create a node

opening.argument: Judge, the income figures should be read as a calculation using a changing token price, not a guaranteed dollar payout. The presenter says the cost is subject to change, explains that the ten tokens used to create a node are gone forever, and discloses both gas fees and a monthly maintenance fee. Those are material qualifications for someone considering the figures. His enthusiasm is clear, but enthusiasm does not erase the explicit costs and uncertainty he gives viewers.

citations.quote: that's ten strong tokens uh again this is subject to change
those 10 strong tokens are gone forever
there are insane amounts of gas fees
there is a monthly maintenance fee of about 15 bucks

rebuttal.rebuttal: The opening rightly identifies a strong recommendation and an invitation to discuss partnering. But its quotes about money-making do not establish a guaranteed payout: the stated reward is denominated in STRONG, while the dollar figure depends on the token price. Nor is the purchase described as recoverable; the presenter expressly says the tokens are gone forever. The paid alerts are a separate offering, not evidence that the node's stated reward has already been paid.

citations.quote: with a node reward goal of 0.1 strong per full day that a node is running
those 10 strong tokens are gone forever
Literally it's $9 a month guys you can sign up down below

true_side_reply.rebuttal: Disclosing costs does not neutralize the central pitch. The presenter converts the reward goal into '$100 every single day,' calls the earnings scenario probable, and urges viewers with money to consider a purchase because it 'prints money.' His own warning that the purchase tokens are gone forever makes the promoted recurring return more consequential, not less.

opening.argument: Judge, much of the video walks through how the node arrangement is presented and how the figures are calculated. The presenter identifies the ten-token contribution, explains that those tokens are not returned, and uses the stated daily reward goal to work through the dollar estimate. He also says he will not cover the node setup in this video. That is a limited explanation of a product and its arithmetic, not a demonstration that viewers have received the projected income.

I'm not going to get into how to set up a node because that is a whole video in itself

rebuttal.rebuttal: The prosecution points to sales language, but that does not make the intervening walkthrough disappear. The presenter examines the required contribution and the reward calculation, then discusses setup costs. Even his invitation to partner asks viewers to start a conversation by DM; the quoted invitation does not itself show a completed transaction or a realized return.

true_side_reply.rebuttal: The calculations are the vehicle for the solicitation, not a detached lesson. The presenter says one node will make '$100 a day, every single day,' strongly recommends the purchase as something that 'prints money,' and offers to run a node for viewers who DM him. A completed transaction is not required to recognize the promotional pitch.

if you want me to run a node for you, all you got to do is send me an Instagram DM

opening.argument: Judge, the described transaction is a purchase through a named node application, with stated token and maintenance costs. The presenter describes swapping Ethereum for STRONG, connecting to the app, and buying a node. His separate paid offering is identified as buy-and-sell alerts. The partnership invitation is to discuss running a node by DM; the supplied account does not show a request for wallet credentials, a referral downline, or a viewer sending funds to him. Those missing steps matter when deciding what mechanism this video actually establishes.

you would need to contribute ten of the strong tokens to create a node
You have to swap your Ethereum into the Strong Token then you have to connect onto this DAPF then you have to buy the node
if you want me to run a node for you, all you got to do is send me an Instagram DM
if you want to get my buy and sell signals, if you want to know my alerts

rebuttal.rebuttal: The prosecution's quotes establish an aggressive pitch for a paid node, an alerts subscription, and a DM invitation. They do not establish that the presenter takes custody of a viewer's tokens or that the DM results in a deposit to him. The purchase instructions instead describe acquiring STRONG and connecting to the node application. Judge the observed transaction, without filling in unshown steps.

citations.quote: You have to swap your Ethereum into the Strong Token then you have to connect onto this DAPF then you have to buy the node
send me a DM and say, Radhiz, I want to partner with you on a node

true_side_reply.rebuttal: The concern does not depend on a credential request or a payment directly to the presenter. He says creating a node requires ten STRONG tokens, promotes recurring passive dollars from that paid node, and invites viewers to have him run one for them. The ordinary purchase steps are precisely how viewers would enter the promoted earning arrangement.
